seoTitle: Free IEEE 754 Float to Hex and Binary Converter
metaDescription: Convert numbers to 32-bit and 64-bit IEEE 754 hex and bits, with sign, exponent and mantissa, or decode a hex pattern. Free, in your browser.
intro: Enter a number to see its 32-bit and 64-bit IEEE 754 representation in hex and binary, split into sign, exponent and mantissa, or decode a hex pattern.
why:
Floating-point numbers store a sign, an exponent and a fraction, which is why 0.1 cannot be held exactly and why 0.1 plus 0.2 is not 0.3. Seeing the actual bits explains many surprises: rounding in a financial report, NaN handling in a network protocol, or a value that shows up as 0x3f800000 in a memory dump.

Type one value per line, such as 0.1, -118.625, NaN or 1e300. The tool prints the float32 and float64 hex, the bit groups and the stored value after rounding to single precision. Paste 0x40490fdb to decode it as a float32, or a longer pattern as float64.
howTo: Enter one number or hex pattern per line, such as 0.1 or 0x40490fdb.
Read the hex and the sign, exponent and mantissa bits for 32 and 64 bits.

faq.q: How does it decide between 32 and 64-bit hex input?
faq.a: Up to eight hex digits are read as a 32-bit float and up to sixteen digits as a 64-bit double. Longer patterns are rejected.

faq.q: Why does the stored 32-bit value differ from my number?
faq.a: Single precision has only about seven significant decimal digits, so the nearest representable value is shown. 0.1 becomes roughly 0.10000000149.

faq.q: Does it show half precision or bfloat16?
faq.a: No. Only the 32-bit and 64-bit formats are supported, because those cover most programming languages, databases and memory dumps. Half precision and bfloat16 are not included.
NaN, Infinity and -Infinity are accepted, as are numbers in exponent form like 1e300. Zero shows the sign bit, so negative zero can be told apart from zero.
